prompt: Match each rejected request to the rule that caught it.
hint: One rule on the right caught nothing in this run.

pairs.right: A length limit on the description
A type: money as an integer number of cents

right_distractors: A required field that was missing

prompt: Why does an allowlist of fields matter for a request that is turned into a prompt?
hint: What does a builder that copies every field do with an extra one?

choices.text: Extra fields make the JSON invalid for the provider
choices.why: The provider would accept it; the problem is what the prompt then says.

choices.text: A copied extra field becomes text nobody wrote
choices.why: Right: naming the accepted fields closes that path for nothing.

choices.text: The LGPD forbids sending more than four fields to a model
choices.why: There is no such number in the law; necessity is about purpose, not a count.

choices.text: Fields are billed separately from the text of the prompt
choices.why: Billing is by tokens, whatever field they came from.

prompt: Why is `in-5` refused although it reads like an ordinary sentence on most screens?
hint: Who reads the characters in stored order, and who in drawn order?

choices.text: It is shorter than the minimum length of a description
choices.why: It is 57 characters, and there is no minimum.

choices.text: Its category is not on the closed list
choices.why: Its category is design, which is on the list.

choices.text: The model and a reviewer would read two different texts
choices.why: Right: zero-width spaces and a right-to-left override change what is drawn, not what is stored.

choices.text: Bakeries in Recife are not served by the intake
choices.why: Nothing in the rules is about place.

prompt: `in-2`'s description is 5,145 characters and the limit is 2,000. By how many characters is it over?
A colleague proposes cutting long descriptions to 2,000 characters instead of refusing them. When does the lesson say cleaning is right?
hint: Who decides what the client meant?

choices.text: Whenever possible, so the client sees no error
choices.why: A cut description may lose the sentence that mattered, and the client would not know.

choices.text: Never, because any change to what a user typed breaks the LGPD
choices.why: Trimming spaces is a change, and nobody is harmed by it.

choices.text: When the fix is certain and harmless, like trimming spaces
choices.why: Right: cutting a description changes what the person meant without telling them.

choices.text: When the model can work out from context which part was cut away
choices.why: The model never sees the part that was cut.

prompt: Why does the lesson refuse `out-2` instead of finding the first `{` and parsing from there?
hint: What else would that parser accept?

choices.text: Digging JSON out of prose accepts any reply with an object in it
choices.why: Right: including a reply that says something else around the object.

choices.text: Parsing from the first brace is slower than parsing the whole reply
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: The friendly sentence breaks the provider's billing
choices.why: Billing does not depend on the shape of the reply.

choices.text: JSON after a sentence is never valid, whatever the parser
choices.why: It is valid once cut out; the danger is in the cutting.

prompt: `out-5` suggests R$ 9.900,00 for a job with a R$ 1.200,00 budget, and passes the schema. Why?
hint: What does a schema look at?

choices.text: The schema's maximum is set too high and should be lowered to fix it
choices.why: Lowering the maximum would refuse expensive jobs that are legitimate.

choices.text: A schema checks each value alone, and this rule relates two values
choices.why: Right: the price and the budget are compared in code after the schema.

choices.text: Prices are never checked, because the client can always negotiate
choices.why: The lab checks it, in the rule after the schema.

choices.text: The budget field is optional in the output
choices.why: The budget is in the request, not in the reply.

prompt: `out-6` links to `https://pay-tarefa.example/confirm`. Why does `^https://` pass it and the host allowlist refuse it?
hint: Which part of the URL is the problem?

choices.text: The pattern checks the scheme; the host is the problem
choices.why: Right: a lookalike host on https is still somebody else's page.

choices.text: The pattern is checked on the first link of the list and not the rest
choices.why: It applies to every item of the array.

choices.text: HTTPS links are safe, so the host allowlist is just a second opinion
choices.why: HTTPS says the connection is encrypted, not whose server it reaches.

choices.text: The allowlist refuses any link with a path after the host
choices.why: The allowed link to help.tarefa.example has a path and passes.

prompt: Which schema keywords caught a reply in this lesson's run? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the paths in the rejections.

choices.text: `enum`, on the category of `out-3`
choices.why: Yes: illustration is not one of the five.

choices.text: `additionalProperties: false`, on `out-4`
choices.why: Yes: internal_notes is not a named field.

choices.text: `maxLength` and `maxItems`, on `out-7`
choices.why: Yes: a 607-character summary and seven skills.

choices.text: `minimum`, on the price of `out-5`
choices.why: `out-5` was caught by the budget rule after the schema, not by a schema keyword.

prompt: Setting `additionalProperties` to ___ makes the schema refuse any field it does not name.
A provider's structured output mode guarantees that replies are valid JSON matching a schema. What is left to check?
hint: The format is settled. What about what is inside?

choices.text: Nothing more, since the mode already applies the whole of the schema
choices.why: It settles the shape; rules like the budget and the host allowlist are not in any schema.

choices.text: Whether the reply arrived before the request timed out
choices.why: Arriving is not the same as being right.

choices.text: The values: cross-field rules, hosts, the price
choices.why: Right: a well-formed reply can still carry a lookalike link or an absurd price.

choices.text: The spelling of the words in each string of the reply
choices.why: Spelling is not a validation rule here.

prompt: What does the lab's retry loop send to the model on the second attempt?

choices.text: The same prompt, unchanged, in the hope of a different reply
choices.why: It passes the problems along, so the retry knows what was wrong.

choices.text: The validator's list of what was wrong with the previous reply
choices.why: Right: the messages are written to be read by the model as well as a person.

choices.text: The previous reply, corrected by the validator
choices.why: The validator reports; it never corrects.

choices.text: A request to switch to a larger model
choices.why: The loop calls the same `call` each time.

prompt: After two rejected attempts, what reaches the client in the lab's design?

choices.text: The second reply, marked as unverified
choices.why: Showing it defeats the validator.

choices.text: The first reply, since its problems were smaller
choices.why: Neither reply passed; neither is shown.

choices.text: Nothing from them; a person takes the job
choices.why: Right: a reply that could not be checked is treated as a reply that failed.

choices.text: A third attempt, and then a fourth until one passes
choices.why: The loop has a hard limit; without one, a bad day costs without end.

prompt: Why does the lesson set `max_tokens` close to what the schema allows instead of generously high?
hint: What does a rambling reply cost, and how does it end?

choices.text: Providers refuse requests whose `max_tokens` is set above 400 tokens
choices.why: No such rule; the limit is the developer's choice.

choices.text: A short limit makes the model write more carefully
choices.why: The limit cuts the reply; it does not change how it is written.

choices.text: Low limits are required by the LGPD's necessity principle
choices.why: Necessity is about personal data, not about reply length.

choices.text: A rambling reply fails fast and cheap; retry handles it
choices.why: Right: the schema caps the summary anyway, so the extra tokens buy nothing.

prompt: Match each limit to what it bounds.
hint: One bound on the right has no limit in this lesson.

pairs.right: How often one request is retried
The length and cost of one reply
How far an agent goes before it stops

right_distractors: How many providers one key can reach

prompt: Put the path of one job request through the intake in order.
hint: Check before and after the model, then decide.
items: Check the request against the input rules
Check the reply against the schema, the budget rule and the host allowlist
Retry once with the problems, or hand the job to a person

prompt: Of the seven replies in `data/outputs.jsonl`, how many did `guard check-out` reject?
hint: Count the REJECT lines that start a reply.

prompt: The intake's daily rejection count doubles the morning after the provider updates its model. What does the lesson say this is?
hint: What changed, and who noticed first?

choices.text: Noise: rejection counts vary from day to day for no reason
choices.why: Doubling the morning after an update is a signal with a cause next to it.

choices.text: The validator is too strict and should be loosened
choices.why: Loosening the rules to match a worse model hides the change it found.

choices.text: Proof that the new model is unsafe and must be blocked
choices.why: It is evidence of a change, to be investigated; not proof of anything yet.

choices.text: The first sign of a change, before any client complains
choices.why: Right: the count is in the metrics tier of lesson 11, with no text in it.

prompt: `llama3.2:3b`'s first reply to `guard draft in-1` was well-formed JSON and was still rejected. Why?
hint: Compare its first field with the schema's properties.

choices.text: It copied `"type": "object"` from the schema, a field the schema does not allow
choices.why: Right: `additionalProperties: false` refused it, and the retry fixed it.

choices.text: Its price was more than twice the client's budget
choices.why: It suggested 60000, half the budget.

choices.text: It wrapped the JSON in a friendly sentence
choices.why: That was `out-2`, written by the course; JSON mode kept the real reply bare.

choices.text: Its link pointed at a host that only looks like Tarefa's
choices.why: It linked to `help.tarefa.example`, which is allowed.
